html:
Tunisia is the smallest country of the Maghreb, at the point where Africa reaches closest to Sicily. The map shows it from 1900 to 2010: as a French protectorate until 1956, then as an independent state.

The land has a long past: Carthage, the Roman province of Africa, the Aghlabid and Hafsid dynasties, and then the Ottoman Beylik of Tunis. In 1881 France made it a protectorate. The bey stayed on his throne, but French officials ran the country and French and Italian settlers took land. In 1942 and 1943 it was a battleground of the Second World War.

The nationalist lawyer Habib Bourguiba led the independence movement. Tunisia became independent in 1956, and a republic in 1957 with Bourguiba as president. He pushed a secular programme: schooling for all, and a family law of 1956 that banned polygamy and gave women the right to divorce. He also ruled as a one-party leader for thirty years.

In 1987 Zine El Abidine Ben Ali removed him and ruled until 2011. In December 2010 a street vendor, Mohamed Bouazizi, set himself on fire in protest. The protests that followed drove Ben Ali out and set off the Arab Spring across the region. Tunisia then built the region's most lasting democracy, though from 2021 President Kais Saied took most power into his own hands.
